props.title: Metropolis
props.initialSlug: Futuristic city divided between workers and elite

sections.content: Metropolis (1927) stands as Fritz Lang's masterpiece of German Expressionism, revolutionizing sci-fi cinema with its towering Art Deco cityscapes and groundbreaking practical effects. The film's stark class divide between workers underground and elites in skyscrapers influenced every dystopian film that followed, from Blade Runner (1982) to Snowpiercer (2013). Lang's innovative use of the Schüfftan process - using mirrors to combine miniature sets with live actors - created impossible architecture that still amazes nearly 100 years later.

sections.content: The film's influence on visual style cannot be overstated. The machine-human "Maria" robot directly inspired C-3PO's design in Star Wars (1977), while the city's stratified architecture echoes through Brazil (1985), The Fifth Element (1997), and Elysium (2013). The famous sequence of workers marching in mechanical unison influenced everything from Modern Times (1936) to Pink Floyd: The Wall (1982).

Beyond aesthetics, Metropolis established core themes of sci-fi cinema: class warfare, automation anxiety, and the dehumanization of workers. These ideas resurface in Alphaville (1965), THX 1138 (1971), and High-Rise (2015). The film's religious imagery and warnings about technological progress influenced later German Expressionist works like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) and continue through modern dystopian films. sections.content: The film's complex restoration history mirrors its themes of preservation versus progress. The 2010 restoration, incorporating footage found in Argentina, finally brought the film close to Lang's original vision. This 148-minute version reveals previously lost subplots that strengthen the parallel between the Tower of Babel allegory and the film's critique of industrial capitalism, themes later explored in Playtime (1967) and Silent Running (1972).
